title: A new compound burns fat without the muscle loss of popular weight-loss drugs
summary:
GLP-1 medications like Ozempic and Wegovy have revolutionized obesity treatment, but they come with a catch: they can cause muscle loss and other side effects. Now, researchers at UC Berkeley are exploring a completely different strategy—one that doesn't just cut calories but boosts the body's energy burn.

In a study published August 21 in Science Advances, the team reports that a compound called TOFA (5-tetradecyloxy-2-furoic acid) can interfere with lipid production while activating genes that encourage cells to burn fat for fuel. In mice, TOFA improved insulin sensitivity, reduced triglycerides, and improved fatty liver disease—all while preserving lean muscle mass.

"Body weight responds to two levers: taking in fewer calories, or spending more energy," said senior author Anders Näär. "GLP-1s work almost entirely on the first, so we went after the second."

TOFA was first discovered in the 1970s and belongs to a class of compounds called ACC inhibitors. Many of these have entered clinical trials but none have been approved, partly because they can raise triglyceride levels. TOFA, however, behaves differently: it also activates receptors called PPARα and PPARδ, which switch on genes for fat uptake and burning. In mice, this increased energy use by up to 18% without making the animals more active or raising their body temperature.

Interestingly, combining TOFA with GLP-1 drugs like semaglutide (Ozempic) or tirzepatide (Mounjaro) produced even better results than either alone. "TOFA worked additively or synergistically with the GLP-1 appetite-suppressing drugs," Näär said. "We view it as complementary rather than as a replacement."

Despite the promise, TOFA has only been tested in animals. Its safety and effectiveness in humans remain unknown. But this research opens a new avenue for treating obesity and diabetes—one that might avoid the muscle loss that worries many patients.
why_it_matters: This matters because obesity and diabetes affect millions of people, and the most popular new drugs come with a real trade-off — losing muscle along with fat. A future treatment that preserves muscle while helping the body burn energy could improve both long-term health and quality of life for many patients.

background_read: UC Berkeley is a large public research university in California.
GLP-1 drugs such as Ozempic and Wegovy (brand names for semaglutide) mimic a natural gut hormone and were originally developed for diabetes before becoming famous for weight loss.
TOFA is an experimental molecule first discovered in the 1970s that belongs to a class called ACC inhibitors, which block the body from making fats.
In this study, TOFA activated proteins called PPARα and PPARδ that turn on fat-burning genes, and combining it with semaglutide or tirzepatide (Mounjaro) appeared to work even better in mice.
ACC inhibitors have gone through clinical trials before, but none has been approved — partly because some raised triglyceride levels.

perspectives.description: For patients, a drug that burns fat without sacrificing muscle would address one of the biggest concerns about GLP-1 therapies. The study also shows that combining TOFA with existing drugs could work better than either approach alone.

TOFA and related ACC inhibitors have a rocky history — many have gone to clinical trials but none has been approved. Mouse results often fail to translate to humans, so excitement should be tempered until safety and effectiveness are tested in people.

The research highlights that weight loss is about two levers, calorie intake and energy output, and most successful drugs pull only one. Identifying a complementary mechanism is scientifically valuable even if TOFA itself never becomes a medicine.

The next steps will be clinical trials to see whether TOFA is safe, whether it raises triglycerides in humans, and whether it truly protects muscle. If those questions are answered, it could lead to a new generation of combination therapies for obesity and diabetes.
